html:
Two dynasties founded by peoples from the northeast that ruled northern China alongside the Song: the Liao of the Khitan people, from 916 to 1125, and the Jin of the Jurchen people, from 1115 to 1234.

Liao. The Khitan leader Abaoji founded the state in 916. It held Manchuria, Mongolia and a strip of northern China around modern Beijing. The Song failed to take that strip back and, in 1005, agreed to pay the Liao a yearly tribute of silver and silk. The Liao ran a dual government: one for the nomads in their own way and one for farmers on the Chinese model.

Jin. The Jurchen, once Liao subjects, rose under Wanyan Aguda in 1115. They allied with the Song to crush the Liao, then turned on the Song. In 1127 they took the Song capital Kaifeng and captured two emperors. The Song court fled south, and the Huai River became the border. Part of the Liao elite fled west and founded the Western Liao in Central Asia.

The Jin rulers adopted Chinese ways, revived Confucian learning and even repaired the Great Wall. It did not save them. Genghis Khan invaded in 1211, and after more than twenty years of war the Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234. The Jurchen later returned to history as the Manchus, founders of the Qing.

These states show a pattern in Chinese history: frontier peoples who took over the north and learned to rule farmers without giving up their own identity. The Yuan and Qing followed the same path on a larger scale.
sum: Two dynasties founded by peoples from the northeast that ruled northern China alongside the Song: the Liao of the Khitan people, from 916 to 1125, and the Jin of the Jurchen people, from 1115 to 1234.
